title: Your first franchise visit: look beyond the front counter
excerpt: A store visit becomes more useful when you pay attention to the work behind the customer experience.
imageAlt: An entrepreneur visits the working kitchen and storage area of a café with its manager.
introHighlight: A well-presented outlet can tell you something about a brand. A conversation about how it operates can tell you much more. Treat your first visit as a chance to understand an ordinary working day, rather than a tour of the finished interiors.

sections.heading: Visit with a short set of questions
body: Before you arrive, write down what you need to understand: your role in the business, the people required to run it, and the tasks that need attention every day. Tell the operator what you would like to discuss and arrange a suitable time. A planned conversation is more useful than trying to interview someone during a busy service.

Ask whether the location is company-operated or franchise-operated. That distinction helps you understand whose experience you are hearing. One outlet is a useful starting point, but it cannot represent every location or every operator.

sections.heading: Follow the work behind the sale
body: Watch the customer journey, then ask about the preparation behind it. How is stock received? Who checks quality? How are shifts planned? What happens when a piece of equipment stops working? The point is to understand what the operating model requires from people and systems.

A café might look calm at the counter while a small team handles deliveries, preparation and online orders elsewhere. A retail store may depend on regular stock transfers that are invisible to a casual visitor. Ask for an explanation of these routines rather than assuming that the visible activity is the whole business.
bullets: What must be completed before the outlet opens?
Which decisions can the manager make independently?
What does the team do when demand is higher or lower than expected?
Which issues require support from the brand?

sections.heading: Separate observations from claims
body: Keep two columns in your notes: what you saw and what you still need to verify. A busy half-hour is an observation. It is not evidence of average sales, profitability or likely results at another location. Ask for the relevant records and current proposal through the appropriate channels.

Respect staff, customer privacy and the operator’s time. Ask before taking photographs, recording a discussion or entering non-public areas. Useful due diligence does not require interrupting the business.

sections.heading: Leave with a better next conversation
body: After the visit, identify three questions that remain unanswered. You might need to understand staffing, compare a different format or speak with another operator. Send a concise follow-up rather than immediately turning the visit into a decision.
A good visit makes your shortlist more informed. It should help you explain why a business may suit your circumstances—and what you still need to learn before moving ahead.

title: Before a second location, test how your first runs without you
excerpt: A practical way to spot the decisions and routines that still depend on the founder.
imageAlt: A founder watches her homeware shop team serve customers and organise products independently.
introHighlight: When you are considering expansion, ask how the existing outlet works when you are not making every decision. A short, planned test can reveal the processes your next location will need.

sections.heading: Start with an ordinary week
body: Choose a representative period and agree on the test with your manager. Keep the usual staffing and trading conditions. The purpose is to understand the current business, not to create a perfect week with additional people and unusually close supervision.

Set clear boundaries. Decide what the manager may resolve, what requires approval, and which incidents need immediate escalation. You remain responsible for the business; this is a test of operating independence, not a reason to withdraw support.

sections.heading: Keep a decision log
body: Ask the team to record the decisions they needed help with. Capture the issue, the information they had, the person who resolved it and what would have made the decision easier. This gives you specific material to improve instead of a general impression that the outlet needs you.
bullets: Routine decisions: shifts, replenishment, handovers and closing checks.
Customer exceptions: complaints, refunds and service recovery.
Supplier issues: delays, substitutions and quality concerns.
Escalations: safety incidents, equipment failures and decisions outside delegated authority.

sections.heading: Turn recurring questions into usable guidance
body: Look for patterns when you review the log. If the same question appears repeatedly, the answer may need to become a checklist, a clear limit or a short training exercise. A long operations manual will not solve a problem if the team cannot quickly find the instruction it needs.

Test each improvement in the outlet. Ask a colleague to use the new checklist without your explanation. If it still depends on knowledge that only you hold, revise it. Record who owns the guidance and how updates will reach the team.

sections.heading: Use the findings to plan the next location
body: Review both the outcomes and the support the team needed. Where were delays? Which responsibilities were unclear? Did the manager have enough information and authority to act? Avoid judging the test only by whether you received fewer calls.

The exercise does not prove that a business is ready to franchise. It gives you a clearer starting point for discussing training, management capacity, operating standards and the support required by another location. Expansion planning becomes more useful when it begins with the way your business actually works.

title: A useful franchise enquiry starts with a clear brief
excerpt: The details that help turn an initial enquiry into a relevant conversation about your options.
imageAlt: A couple writes down business requirements and reviews information on a laptop at home.
introHighlight: You do not need to have every answer before making an enquiry. A short brief about your circumstances helps the conversation focus on suitable options and the information you still need.

sections.heading: Describe the role you want to play
body: Start with your available time and the work you are willing to do. Do you expect to be present at the outlet, employ a manager or explore a company-operated arrangement? These are different responsibilities, and a brand name alone does not tell you which one applies.

Explain your relevant experience without feeling that you need to sound like an expert. Experience in customer service, people management, retail or another business can help shape the discussion. If this would be your first business, say so.

sections.heading: Be specific about your location
body: Share the city or locality you are considering and whether you already have a property. If you do, provide the approximate area, frontage, floor and access conditions. Do not assume a property is suitable just because it is vacant or well located.

If you have not chosen a site, that is useful information too. The discussion can begin with the type of location and catchment a format requires. Ask about current territory availability before making commitments around a particular property.

sections.heading: State your investment assumptions
body: Give an indicative budget range and explain what you expect it to cover. A quote for the franchise fee or store setup may not answer questions about deposits, opening stock, tax, working capital and a reserve for unexpected costs. Request a current, itemised proposal.

Avoid sending financial account details or sensitive documents in an initial message. Start with the information needed to assess fit, and agree on a suitable process if supporting documents are required later.

sections.heading: Use a simple opening brief
body: A useful first message can be short: “I am exploring a business in [locality]. I can be involved [full time / through a manager / to be discussed]. My indicative budget is [range], and I [have / do not have] a property. I would like to understand the available formats and the complete requirements.”

Add your intended timing and two or three questions that matter most. It is fine to write “I am still deciding” where necessary. The purpose is to make the next conversation relevant, not to commit before you have the evidence to decide.

title: Who runs the outlet? Ask about a working day
excerpt: Look beyond model abbreviations and map the responsibilities that matter in practice.
imageAlt: Two café managers discuss a shift handover beside the service counter.
introHighlight: Model labels such as FOFO, FOCO and FICO can help start a conversation. Your understanding should come from the actual division of work, authority, costs and risk described in the proposal and agreement.

sections.heading: Walk through opening, trading and closing
body: Ask the brand to explain an ordinary day at the proposed outlet. Who opens the premises, checks stock, schedules staff and monitors service? Who reviews the closing reports and follows up on an unresolved issue?

Use the same set of questions for each opportunity. It is easier to compare clear responsibilities than broad statements about how much support is included. Where a brand offers more than one format, ask which answers apply to the specific proposal you are reviewing.

sections.heading: Separate doing the work from paying for it
body: The person managing an activity may not be the person funding it or approving changes. An outlet manager may schedule staff while another party approves headcount. A brand may arrange a supplier while the outlet pays the invoice. Clarify each part separately.
bullets: Who can approve a change or exception?
Who receives the records and checks the outcome?

sections.heading: Discuss what happens when something goes wrong
body: Routine operations are only part of the picture. Ask how the parties handle an unexpected closure, an equipment failure, a complaint or a staffing gap. Understand the escalation route and what support is included.

Request examples of the process rather than promises that problems will never occur. Ask how responsibilities change if the outlet needs additional funds or is performing below expectations. Have the relevant advisers review the written terms before you commit.

sections.heading: Create a responsibility map you can explain
body: Summarise the discussion in a simple table and ask the brand to confirm it against the current documents. Mark anything that is still unclear. Treat this summary as a working aid, not a substitute for the agreement.

If you can explain who operates the outlet, who controls the key decisions and what remains your responsibility, you are in a better position to judge whether that format fits your circumstances. If the explanation still depends entirely on an acronym, continue the conversation.
